overview:
A town grew up on a spur of old lava above the mouth of the river Sarno, in Campania, sometime around the seventh or sixth century BCE, in a landscape already worked by Oscan-speaking farmers. Its position — a small port at the head of a river route into the interior, within sight of the Greek colonies across the bay — made it a place where influences collected rather than one that shaped events. Greeks and Etruscans both left their mark on its early sanctuaries and street plan; Samnite hill peoples took control of the region in the later fifth century BCE and built much of the town later visitors would walk through. Pompeii allied with Rome, then joined the Italian revolt against it, and was besieged by Sulla in 89 BCE; the artillery scars are still visible near the Herculaneum Gate. Around 80 BCE it was refounded as a colony of Roman veterans, Colonia Cornelia Veneria Pompeianorum, and Latin displaced Oscan in public life. By the first century CE it was a prosperous provincial town of perhaps eleven to twenty thousand people — estimates vary widely and rest on counting households — living off wine, oil, fish sauce, wool and the trade of a crowded coast dotted with the seaside villas of wealthy Romans.

A severe earthquake in 62 CE brought down much of the town, and rebuilding was still under way when Vesuvius erupted seventeen years later. The eruption ran in two stages: a column of pumice and ash driven tens of kilometres into the sky for the better part of a day, burying Pompeii under nearly three metres of debris and collapsing roofs, followed by pyroclastic surges of superheated gas and rock that swept down the mountain and killed anyone still inside. Pliny the Younger, watching from Misenum as a teenager, wrote the only surviving eyewitness account, in two letters composed for Tacitus some twenty-five years later. His description of a cloud shaped like an umbrella pine gave volcanologists the term "Plinian." The date has traditionally been given as 24 August, on the strength of Pliny's text, but the manuscripts are corrupt at exactly that point, and autumn fruit, heavier clothing, braziers in use and a charcoal graffito in Regio V dated to mid-October have pushed many specialists toward a date in October or early November 79. Around eleven hundred bodies have been recovered at Pompeii; most inhabitants seem to have fled during the first phase, though how many died in the wider region is unknown.

The town was found by accident — the engineer Domenico Fontana cut a water channel through it in 1592 and said nothing — and dug in earnest from 1748, its identity confirmed by an inscription in 1763. Early excavation was closer to treasure hunting; the discipline came later, above all with Giuseppe Fiorelli, who from the 1860s dug stratigraphically and worked out that pouring plaster into the voids left in the ash by decayed bodies would recover their shapes at the moment of death. Roughly a third of the site has never been excavated, deliberately left for better techniques, and much of what has been uncovered has weathered badly under rain, tourism and wartime bombing; UNESCO warned in 2013 that the site risked being listed as endangered before a major EU-funded conservation programme was pushed through.
significance: More than any other site, Pompeii is where the ancient world stops being a matter of monuments and elite literature and becomes a place where people ate, argued, cheated, advertised and voted. Because the ash sealed an ordinary town in a single afternoon rather than letting it decay over centuries, it preserved things almost no other Roman site retains — painted walls in full colour, shop counters, garden root cavities, loaves in ovens, and some eleven thousand painted and scratched inscriptions in which shopkeepers, enslaved people, children and canvassers speak in their own hands. That evidence underwrites much of what modern scholarship believes about Roman urban life, domestic religion, slavery, diet and literacy. Its rediscovery also reshaped European taste: the wall paintings and furnishings that emerged from the eighteenth-century digs fed directly into neoclassicism, and the plaster casts of the dying, first shown to the public in the 1860s, fixed an image of catastrophe that has run through painting, novels and film ever since. Pompeii is simultaneously archaeology's richest single dataset for everyday antiquity and, through two and a half centuries of clumsy digging and exposure, one of its longest-running lessons in how excavation destroys what it reveals.
coverage: Written from general reference and encyclopaedic accounts of the site and the eruption; the dataset itself holds no events for this story, so nothing here is anchored to a mapped point. The thin parts are real ones: the pre-Roman centuries are known almost entirely from archaeology, with no local narrative source; population figures and death tolls are estimates with wide error bars; the eruption date is genuinely unsettled between the traditional 24 August and an autumn date; and Pliny's letters, written decades later and about his uncle rather than the town, are the sole surviving eyewitness testimony, with no voice at all from anyone inside Pompeii on the day.
